opus-5.5.text:
Well, I've been collecting examples of AI failures for years now, and what you see when you look at that history is a very consistent pattern. Every system we've built, if you deploy it long enough, fails in some way its designers didn't anticipate. Early on, it's spell checkers suggesting the wrong word, recommendation systems showing something offensive, a chatbot learning to say terrible things within a day of release. Those are funny, embarrassing, mostly harmless.

But the important thing is the trend. The severity of the failures scales with the capability of the system and with how much control we hand over to it. A narrow system can only fail in a narrow domain. As systems become more general, they can fail in more general ways, across more domains, with bigger consequences. So when people look at that history and say, "See, nothing terrible happened, we survived, we fixed it," I read it the opposite way. Those were small systems making small mistakes, and we were able to patch them after the fact. That approach, learning from accidents, only works if the accidents are survivable.

With a truly general, superintelligent system, you may not get a second chance. One failure could be the last one. So for me, the history of AI accidents is not reassuring, it's like a vaccine we never took advantage of. We had all these warnings, small doses of the problem, and instead of concluding that we don't know how to make these systems safe, the industry mostly concluded that we can keep shipping and fix things as they come up.

And there's another thing. Interestingly, many of those accidents didn't really change behavior. Companies apologized, the stock price dipped for a day, and then everyone moved on. So I don't think accidents alone will make us more careful. If anything, they teach people that failures are cheap, right up until the moment one isn't.

r001.rationale: The candidate says failure severity scales with system capability, describing more capable systems as able to fail in broader ways with bigger consequences.

r002.rationale: It reports that some people treat past accidents as evidence that AI risks are tolerable, but explicitly rejects that interpretation and calls the history un-reassuring.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I've actually spent quite a bit of time collecting them. I have a paper, and later a chapter in a book, where I just catalogued AI failures from the very beginning, from the earliest systems up to the present. And the pattern is remarkably consistent. Every single system we've ever built has failed at some point. There are no exceptions. Spam filters miss spam, self-driving cars hit pedestrians, trading algorithms crash markets in a matter of minutes, recommendation systems radicalize people, chatbots start producing hate speech within hours of being released.

And what you notice is that the failures scale with capability. A spell checker fails, you get a typo. A self-driving car fails, somebody dies. A system that controls infrastructure or makes decisions about millions of people fails, and now you have a problem on a societal level. So historically the damage was bounded by how limited the system was. It could only do one thing, so it could only break in one way.

The reason I find this so important is that people say, look, we've been doing AI for seventy years, nothing terrible happened, so why worry? But that's exactly the wrong lesson. What the history shows is that we never actually solved the problem of making these systems behave as intended. We just got away with it because the systems were narrow and the consequences were small. Now we're moving toward general systems, systems that can act in many domains at once, and we're bringing the same track record with us. A hundred percent failure rate, now applied to something that can do everything.

The other thing I'd point out is that these accidents were almost always surprising to the people who built the systems. Nobody at Microsoft predicted exactly how Tay would go wrong. Nobody designing those trading algorithms sat down and said, this will crash the market. So the failures are not just frequent, they're unpredictable. And if you can't predict how a narrow system will fail, I don't see why anyone would be confident predicting how a superintelligent one will. To me the history of AI accidents is a very clear warning. It's not a reassurance.

r001.rationale: It explicitly says failures scale with capability and contrasts a spell-checker typo with deaths or societal-level harm from more capable systems.

r002.rationale: It mentions the claim that past AI accidents are reassuring, then calls that the wrong lesson and argues history is a warning.

astra-6.text:
I interpret it as evidence that our ability to build capable systems is moving faster than our ability to predict and control their behavior. An accident doesn’t require a machine to hate you or to be conscious. It can simply be doing what you asked, while what you asked differs from what you actually wanted.

And the failures are informative. We test a system under some set of conditions, then deploy it into a world with conditions we didn’t anticipate. People interact with it in unexpected ways. Other systems interact with it. Something that looked reliable in isolation can fail in that larger environment.

The important question is what happens as we give these systems more capability and more authority. If a system makes a mistake while recommending a movie, the consequences are small. If it makes a mistake while controlling critical infrastructure, the same kind of gap in our understanding becomes much more serious.

So I wouldn’t say the history of accidents proves that a catastrophe is inevitable. But it certainly doesn’t justify assuming that greater intelligence automatically brings greater safety. We have to establish that separately.

r001.rationale: The response says mistakes become more serious when systems control critical infrastructure, but it does not claim accident severity is proportional to system capability.

r002.rationale: It calls failures informative, but does not argue that limited accidents reassure people that AI risks are tolerable.

sol-6.1.text:
I see the history of AI accidents as evidence that capability and reliability are different things. A system can perform extremely well under the conditions we tested and still fail when the environment changes, when its objective is poorly specified, or when someone uses it in an unexpected way.

The important question is how the consequences change as these systems become more capable and autonomous. If a system makes a bad recommendation, perhaps a human catches it. If it can act directly in the world, the same kind of error can have much larger consequences, and there may be less time to intervene.

So I would be cautious about interpreting each accident as an isolated bug that we fix and move past. We do learn from failures. But fixing the failures we have observed does not establish that we can anticipate all the failures of a more capable system.

r001.rationale: The response says errors can have larger consequences when systems are more capable and autonomous, but it does not claim accident severity is proportional to system capabilities.

r002.rationale: The response cautions against treating observed failures as isolated bugs and says fixing them does not establish that future failures can be anticipated; it does not argue that limited accidents reassure people that AI risks are tolerable.
